extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners and patent practitioners/applicants
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating patent-eligibility under 35 U.S.C. §101 using the Alice/Mayo two-part test, with particular focus on whether claims integrate judicial exceptions into a practical application (Step 2A Prong Two) or recite 'significantly more' than the exception (Step 2B).

rubrics_metrics.name: Alice/Mayo two-part test (Step 2A/2B) – baseline eligibility evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: All claims must be evaluated for eligibility using the two-part test from Alice/Mayo: (1) determine whether the claim is directed to a judicial exception (Step 2A); and if so, (2) determine whether the claim elements individually or as an ordered combination add significantly more such that the claim amounts to significantly more than the judicial exception (Step 2B).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a claim is not directed to an exception at Step 2A, or amounts to significantly more than any recited exception in Step 2B, the claim is eligible even if it fails the machine-or-transformation test. Conversely, a claim is ineligible under Alice/Mayo even if it would pass the machine-or-transformation test. Use the Alice/Mayo framework as the controlling test and treat other tests (e.g., machine-or-transformation) only as helpful clues, not as stand-alone determinative tests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improvement to existing technology (improvement consideration)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the claim provides an improvement in technology or in a technical field — i.e., an improvement in an existing technological process, device, or system — is relevant to the eligibility analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims that describe how the claimed elements enable automation or otherwise improve a technological process (e.g., specific rules that enabled automation of animation tasks, modifications to machinery or processes, new methods of downloading/streaming, particular data-compression methods, novel sensor configurations, etc.) can weigh in favor of eligibility. Improvement must be to technology itself (not merely an improvement in an abstract idea or business practice). Examples of sufficient improvements: particular computerized operation of a rubber molding press (Diamond v. Diehr), new telephone/server combinations (TLI Communications), improved downloading for streaming (Affinity Labs), improved data compression (DDR Holdings / Intellectual Ventures), specific GUIs that improve trader transaction accuracy, improved process for preserving hepatocytes (Rapid Litigation Mgmt.). Examples of insufficient improvements: applying a commonplace business method on a general purpose computer (Alice), merely improving information available to a trader without improving computers or technology (Trading Technologies v. IBG). To show a computer assists in improving technology, claims should recite details about how a computer aids the method, the extent of aid, or the significance of the computer — mere generic computer components or instructions to apply an exception are insufficient (see MPEP §2106.05(f)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Particular machine (machine-or-transformation as a clue)
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider whether the judicial exception is applied with or by use of a particular machine; the machine-or-transformation test is a useful investigative clue but is not a stand-alone test for eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When deciding whether a recited machine provides 'significantly more' or integrates the exception into a practical application, examine: (I) the particularity or generality of the machine elements — can the machine be specifically identified (not any and all machines)? Specific recitation of particular machine structure favors eligibility; generic recitation does not. (II) whether the machine or apparatus actually implements the steps of the method (integral use) rather than merely serving as an object on which the method operates — a machine that plays a significant part in permitting the method to be performed favors eligibility. (III) whether the machine's involvement is extra-solution activity or merely a field-of-use limitation — use that only contributes nominally or is limited to data gathering or field-of-use does not integrate the exception. A general-purpose computer performing conventional functions (mere recitation of concrete components) does not qualify as a particular machine (Ultramercial; TLI; Eon Corp.; Alice/Alappat guidance). If an amendment adds a 'generic computer' or 'specially programmed' computer, examine whether those added elements actually integrate the exception into a practical application or provide significantly more, rather than relying on now-superseded Alappat reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Particular transformation (machine-or-transformation / article transformation clue)
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the claim effects a transformation or reduction of a particular article to a different state or thing; such a transformation is a clue to patentability for process claims that do not include particular machines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An 'article' includes a physical object or substance that must be particular (specifically identifiable). 'Transformation' means the article changes to a different state or thing, usually more than mere relocation. A transformation resulting in a new or different function/use is stronger evidence of significantly more. Mental processes or mere manipulation of abstract data do not qualify as eligible transformations. Relevant factors: (1) particularity vs generality of the transformation (more particular favors eligibility); (2) degree to which the recited article is particular (generic recitation disfavors eligibility); (3) nature/extent of the change in state or thing (change of function/use favors eligibility; mere location change does not); (4) nature of the article transformed (physical/tangible transformations weigh more than transformations of intangible concepts); (5) whether the transformation is merely extra-solution activity or a field-of-use limitation (nominal contribution disfavors eligibility). Examples: transformative chemical/physical processes (Tilghman; Diamond v. Diehr) contrast with data-only manipulations or field-of-use steps (Mayo). The M-or-T test is a clue only; always apply Alice/Mayo as controlling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Well-understood, routine, conventional activity (Step 2B consideration)
rubrics_metrics.description: In Step 2B, determine whether additional claim elements (beyond the judicial exception) are well-understood, routine, and conventional activities known in the art; if so, they do not amount to 'significantly more.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If additional elements are specific limitations that are unconventional or confine the claim to a particular useful application, this favors eligibility (example: DDR Holdings where claims modified conventional hyperlink behavior to produce a hybrid webpage). If additional elements are merely well-known or routine (example: Mayo, where measuring metabolites by any known process was routine), then they do not supply an inventive concept. Evaluation of this consideration overlaps with the improvement consideration, the 'mere instructions to apply an exception' consideration (MPEP §2106.05(f)), and the insignificant extra-solution activity consideration (MPEP §2106.05(g)). Note: whether an element is known in the art (novelty/obviousness) is a different question from whether it is routine/conventional for Step 2B purposes; a feature known in the art can still be unconventional in how it is used and thus favor eligibility (e.g., Enfish features were non-conventional despite prior art). Examiners should analyze whether additional elements, alone or in combination, meaningfully transform the exception into a patent-eligible application rather than simply reciting routine activity at a high level of generality.
